headline: Launched a national AI-for-science research program at the Energy Department
why: It organizes existing Energy Department AI research with no new statute or spending, and a successor would likely keep a science program.

headline: Set up food price-fixing task forces at the Justice Department and FTC
why: It directs antitrust investigations into food prices and burdens no one; a competition-minded successor would likely keep it.

headline: Set up a Justice Department task force to sue states over AI laws
how: Disband the AI lawsuit task force.
why: It cannot itself override state AI laws, since only Congress or the courts can, so it only directs federal agencies to challenge them.

headline: Moved the SEC to curb proxy advisers over diversity and climate votes
why: It directs the SEC to rewrite or rescind rules, so a new order stops the push; any finished rule changes need their own repeal.

sources.label: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance

headline: Declared illicit fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction
why: The label adds no new legal power; it directs prosecutions and cartel-finance sanctions that a successor would likely keep.

headline: Gave federal workers a 1 percent raise for 2026
why: It is the routine annual pay order; revoking it would take money from federal workers and restore nothing.

headline: Set space goals: Moon return by 2028 and a lunar outpost by 2030
why: It mostly continues Artemis and commercial space policy; the space-based missile defense piece is the part to review separately.

headline: Ordered marijuana moved to Schedule III and more cannabis research
why: It pushes rescheduling and medical research that patients and advocates want, and the DEA has already acted on part of it.

headline: Closed federal agencies on December 24 and 26, 2025
why: A holiday closure order that gave federal workers two paid days off and has nothing left to restore.

headline: Barred underperforming defense contractors from buybacks and dividends
why: It ties contractor payouts to delivering on contracts, a populist limit a successor would likely keep; the Senate is weighing a stricter version.

headline: Shielded Venezuelan oil revenue in U.S. custody from creditors and lawsuits
how: End U.S. custody of Venezuelan oil money.
why: An emergency order under IEEPA; revoking it and ending the emergency removes the shield and the Treasury arrangement.

headline: Created a second emergency board in the Long Island Rail Road dispute
why: A routine Railway Labor Act step the president must take when a party asks; it protects the bargaining process and removes no rights.

headline: Gave the Board of Peace immunity from most lawsuits and some taxes
how: Strip the Board of Peace's immunities.
why: Immunity under the International Organizations Immunities Act is a presidential designation, so a revoking order removes it; whether the president had that power is disputed.

headline: Moved to bar Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes
why: A successor would likely keep a limit on large investors buying family homes, and Congress passed a similar bill in June 2026.

headline: Moved to override Los Angeles fire-rebuilding permits with federal control
how: Return rebuild permitting to Los Angeles.
why: A directive to agencies that blames state and local officials; revoking it ends the federal override. Operative sections not confirmed.

headline: Kept the FEMA Review Council alive through March 2026
why: Housekeeping that extended a review council; a later order extended it again and its term has since run out.

headline: Created a White House initiative on addiction treatment and recovery
why: It declares addiction a chronic, treatable disease and sets a national treatment priority, which a successor would likely keep.

headline: Declared a Cuba emergency and threatened tariffs on its oil suppliers
how: End the Cuba oil tariff emergency.
why: An emergency order under IEEPA; the tariffs were ended by Executive Order 14389, but the emergency remains and carries the later Cuba sanctions.

headline: Ordered a route and fast permits for an IndyCar race in Washington, D.C.
why: A one-time event order for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix; it takes nothing from anyone and has no lasting effect after the race.

headline: Authorized tariffs on countries that trade with Iran, since ended
why: Executive Order 14389 ended the duties after the Supreme Court limited emergency tariffs, leaving nothing to undo.

headline: Put commercial arms sales ahead of strategic goals in weapons exports
how: Restore the earlier arms transfer policy.
why: It tells agencies how to rank goals in arms sales and supplements the 2018 policy rather than replacing it, so a signature reorders the priorities.

headline: Dropped the extra 25 percent tariff on India tied to Russian oil
why: It removed a tariff, so reversing it would raise prices; the underlying emergency tariffs were later ended by Executive Order 14389.

headline: Gave Homeland Security access to all Justice Department criminal records
how: Close DHS's access to criminal records.
why: A directive to the Attorney General and DHS; revoking it ends the access, though any foreign data-sharing agreements already signed need separate action.

headline: Ordered the Pentagon to buy power from coal plants under long-term contracts
how: End the Pentagon coal purchase order.
why: It directs the War and Energy Departments to seek long-term contracts; revoking it stops new deals, but signed contracts would run their term.

headline: Used wartime powers to prioritize glyphosate (Roundup) supply
why: A Defense Production Act directive to the Agriculture Department; revoking it ends the priority status, and a Senate bill to block it is only a proposal.

headline: Ended duty-free treatment for small packages from every country
why: Congress's 2025 tax law already ends the small-package exemption in 2027, so reversing the order would only delay a change that is coming.

headline: Ended the emergency tariffs after the Supreme Court limited them
why: It stops collection of duties the Supreme Court's ruling put in doubt; reversing it would only bring the tariffs back.

headline: Ordered a government-wide push against scam centers and online fraud rings
why: It directs reviews and an action plan against transnational scam networks and support for victims; nothing in it takes anything from Americans.

headline: Let the Energy Secretary use wartime production powers on his own
why: Housekeeping that shifts who may use existing Defense Production Act powers; a later order changed it again and no one's rights are touched.

headline: Told the FTC to crack down on false Made in USA labels
why: It aims enforcement at deceptive labels under the FTC's existing rule, which protects shoppers and honest American manufacturers.

headline: Told regulators to ease Dodd-Frank mortgage rules for smaller banks
how: Withdraw the mortgage rule rollback order.
why: It directs regulators to review and revise rules; revoking it stops the push, but any rules already rewritten need their own repeal.

headline: Told the Army and EPA to loosen stormwater and wetlands rules for builders
how: Restore the stormwater and wetlands rules.
why: It directs agencies to revise permits and standards; revoking it stops new rollbacks, but rules already rewritten need their own rulemaking.

headline: Created a Vance-led fraud task force aimed at state benefit programs
why: A task force created by order, so a new order ends it; the fact sheet names Minnesota, California, Illinois, New York, Maine and Colorado.

headline: Ordered an exclusive TV window for the Army-Navy football game
why: It sets a broadcast window for one game and takes nothing from anyone; the FCC license-review hint is worth a separate look.

headline: Extended the FEMA Review Council through May 2026
why: Housekeeping that extended a review council; its term has ended, so there is nothing left to undo.

headline: Banned federal contractors from diversity programs on pain of losing contracts
why: A directive to agencies and the FAR Council to add contract clauses; revoking it stops new clauses, and clauses already written need their own removal.

headline: Ordered citizenship lists and new mail-ballot rules for federal elections
why: A president cannot set election rules by order; a court held the key sections unlawful, but the Supreme Court paused that ruling as premature.

headline: Threatened federal funding to limit college athletes' pay and transfers
why: It directs agencies and cannot bind the NCAA or schools; revoking it ends the funding threats and the push to override state laws.

headline: Fast-tracked psychedelic drug research for serious mental illness
why: It speeds research and approvals for patients who fail standard care, and it approves no drug itself.

headline: Made fixed-price contracts the default for federal purchasing
why: A procurement reform aimed at cost overruns, with exceptions for research; a successor would likely keep it.

headline: Created a federal retirement-account marketplace branded TrumpIRA.gov
how: Take the president's name off the retirement site.
why: It helps workers without employer plans find low-cost IRAs and a savings match; keep the service and rename the site.

headline: Threatened sanctions on foreign banks and firms that do business with Cuba
why: An emergency sanctions program under IEEPA, so revoking the order ends it; the older Cuba embargo rules stay in force regardless.

headline: Told regulators to loosen rules for fintech and crypto firms
how: Withdraw the fintech and crypto rule review.
why: It directs financial regulators to review and revise rules; revoking it stops new loosening, though changes already adopted need their own repeal.

headline: Told banks to treat undocumented customers as a financial risk
how: Withdraw the bank guidance on undocumented customers.
why: It directs Treasury, the CFPB and bank regulators; the June 2026 FinCEN advisory and any rule changes need their own withdrawal.

headline: Ordered fewer recommended childhood vaccines, citing peer countries
why: A presidential directive to health agencies; a court has already stayed the related HHS schedule changes, but the order stands until revoked.

headline: Scrapped the 1972 and 1977 limits on off-road vehicles on public lands
why: It rescinded two older executive orders, so a new order can reissue them; the land laws it points to still apply.

headline: Set up voluntary pre-release security testing for frontier AI models
why: It builds federal cyber defenses and a voluntary framework and expressly creates no licensing, so there is no burden to restore.

headline: Moved roughly 8,000 career federal jobs into a fireable-at-will schedule
how: Return the jobs to civil-service protection.
why: The order moved about 8,000 positions under the rule; the move is a presidential act, but the schedule survives until that rule is replaced.

headline: Ordered stricter rules for importers to stop customs duty evasion
why: It targets importers who underpay or hide their identity, which protects honest businesses and revenue; a successor would likely keep it.

headline: Ordered federal systems to move to quantum-resistant encryption
why: A security upgrade with deadlines in 2030 and 2031 that protects government data; there is nothing to restore.

headline: Ordered a new national quantum strategy and a quantum computing program
why: It sets research and commercialization goals; no one loses anything and a successor would likely continue it.

headline: Ordered support for regenerative farming and fewer chemical crop tools
why: It promotes soil health and research into alternatives to chemicals, goals shared across parties.

headline: Barred waivers that let defense contractors use adversary-nation materials
why: It tightens sourcing rules for military equipment materials from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, which a successor would likely keep.

headline: Moved to pressure the Smithsonian over how it tells American history
why: It responds to a White House report on a museum, which is executive direction; the Smithsonian is governed by its own board.

headline: Created a military spouse commission chaired by the War Secretary's wife
why: An advisory body to recommend help on housing, jobs and child care for military families; it takes nothing from anyone.

headline: Denied birthright citizenship to new groups after losing at the Supreme Court
why: A narrower order issued after the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling against the first; agencies are implementing it, and plaintiffs have asked a court to block it.

headline: Ordered visa denials and revocations for travel to give birth in the U.S.
why: It targets visa misuse for birth tourism and leaves citizenship alone; the citizenship order is the part to undo.

headline: Cut the vaccines recommended for every child and split the MMR shot
how: Restore the full childhood vaccine schedule.
why: A presidential directive with no statutory force; states keep school vaccine rules, and a court had already stayed the related HHS schedule changes.

headline: Restricted new grid equipment from arms-embargoed countries
why: An emergency order on new transformers, inverters and batteries from embargoed nations, a security measure a successor would likely keep; rules are still being written.

headline: Renamed Lake Ontario 'Lake America' in federal records
why: A renaming that binds only federal agencies, so a signature reverses it; it followed the collapse of trade talks with Canada.

headline: Created a commission to plan a NASA-led U.S. Space Academy
why: It only asks a commission to recommend a design; nothing is built or taken from anyone yet.

headline: Ordered tougher meatpacker antitrust enforcement and help for small processors
why: It directs USDA to enforce competition law against meat processors and funds small processors, which a successor would likely keep.

headline: Ordered a review of weakening protections for gray and Mexican wolves
why: Mostly review directives; the wolf delisting review is the part to stop, while the beef origin-label review is one a successor might keep.

headline: Ordered faster Pentagon-to-VA records sharing for veterans' benefits
why: It modernizes records systems so veterans get benefits sooner; no one loses anything.

headline: Split wartime energy production powers between Interior and Energy
why: Housekeeping on who may use existing Defense Production Act powers over energy; it changes no one's rights.

headline: Revoked the 2009 order coordinating Chesapeake Bay cleanup
how: Restore the Chesapeake Bay cleanup order.
why: The 2009 order was an executive order, so a new one can reissue it; the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement is a separate document.

headline: Opened more federal land to hunting and protected lead ammunition
how: Restore the lead ammunition limits on federal land.
why: It sets a presumption that hunting is allowed on federal land, which a successor would likely keep; the lead ammunition piece merits separate review.

headline: Told fisheries managers to weigh recreational fishing equally
why: It expands access for anglers and charter businesses; whether it weakens fish stocks depends on rules not yet written.

headline: Told agencies to weigh employer layoffs when approving H-1B visas
why: It directs scrutiny of sponsors who lay off U.S. workers; the separate $100,000 fee proclamation is the part to review.

headline: Launched America.gov as one AI-powered front door to federal services
why: A single sign-in for services is something a successor would keep; the AI vendors and data handling deserve their own review.

headline: Ordered a Washington, D.C., campaign to cut mosquitoes and ticks
why: A pest-control and disease-research campaign built on non-chemical methods; there is nothing to restore.

headline: Told federal agencies to say 'Super Intelligence' instead of 'AI'
why: A wording change for federal documents that takes nothing from anyone and leaves statutes alone; a successor can drop it whenever.
